lesson.title: In One Set or the Other, Not Both: Symmetric Difference
lesson.summary: The ^ operator (or .symmetric_difference()) collects every element that belongs to exactly one of two sets, excluding anything shared by both.
lesson.body:
You now have three set operations from Set Operations, intersection, and difference: union gathers everything, intersection keeps only what is shared, and difference keeps what one set has that another lacks. Symmetric difference combines the idea behind ordinary difference in both directions at once. It answers: "which elements belong to exactly one of these two sets, but not both."

Python spells this with the ^ operator, borrowed from the same symbol used for exclusive-or in bitwise logic, since the idea is identical: true for one input or the other, never both. The method form is .symmetric_difference(). Unlike ordinary difference, symmetric difference does not care about order, a ^ b always equals b ^ a, because it is really just the union of (a - b) and (b - a).

python_students = {"Alicia", "Bao", "Carmen"}
java_students = {"Bao", "Deion"}

only_one_class = python_students ^ java_students
print(sorted(only_one_class))

manual = (python_students - java_students) | (java_students - python_students)
print(only_one_class == manual)

This prints ['Alicia', 'Carmen', 'Deion'], then True. Bao is excluded from the result because Bao is enrolled in both classes, exactly the case symmetric difference is designed to filter out. Alicia and Carmen appear because they are Python-only, and Deion appears because he is Java-only.

Symmetric difference is a compact way to spot everything that differs between two collections without caring which side each difference came from, useful for tasks like comparing two versions of a guest list and flagging every name that was added or removed, without needing to run difference twice and union the results by hand.
